abstract.title: Abstract
abstract.p: Advanced tumors harboring SWI/SNF mutations are rare and aggressive. Often presenting in young patients, treatment options are limited. This phase II basket study (NCT02601950) assessed oral tazemetostat, an EZH2 inhibitor, at 800 mg twice daily (N = 129). Cohorts included malignant rhabdoid tumors (n = 32, Cohort 1), synovial sarcoma (n = 33, Cohort 2), INI1-negative tumors (n = 32, Cohort 3), renal medullary carcinoma (n = 14, Cohort 4), and poorly differentiated chordoma (n = 18, Cohort 7). Efficacy assessments used a 2-stage Green-Dahlberg design. Stage 1 futility was predefined as objective responses (complete/partial [CR/PR]) <5% (Cohorts 1, 3, 4, 7) or 16-week progression-free survival (PFS) <15% (Cohort 2). Sufficient clinical activity was declared in Stage 2 if ≥5 patients had a CR/PR (Cohorts 1,3,4,7) or ≥9 patients had a CR/PR, or stable disease (Cohort 2; primary endpoints). Responses were observed in malignant rhabdoid tumors (9%; n = 2 PR, n = 1 CR), INI1-negative tumors (9%; n = 3 PR, n = 0 CR), and poorly differentiated chordoma (6%; n = 1 PR, n = 0 CR) but not the remaining 2 cohorts (both 0%). 16-week PFS for synovial sarcoma was 15.2% (n = 5). Grade ≥3 treatment-related adverse events occurred in 10% of patients. Tazemetostat demonstrated preliminary antitumor activity in a subset of poor-prognosis cancers, underscoring the need for combination strategies when EZH2 signaling is not the sole disease driver.

sec.p: Subject terms: Drug development, Cancer prevention

abstract.p: Tumours with alterations in SWI/SNF complex have elevated EZH2 activity, which is associated with poor prognosis and tumour progression. Here, the authors report a phase 2 basket study investigating the safety and efficacy of oral tazemetostat (EZH2 inhibitor) in patients with solid tumours harbouring SWI/SNF driver mutations.

sec.p: Received 2025 Apr 7; Accepted 2026 Feb 6; Collection date 2026.

sec.title: Introduction
sec.p: Epigenetic dysregulation involves heritable changes in gene expression without alterations in the underlying DNA sequence, and this process plays a key role in cancer biology1. Epigenetic abnormalities have been identified across nearly all cancer subtypes1–3. Therefore, drugs targeting epigenetic regulators are of high interest for cancer treatment development4.

Enhancer of zeste homolog 2 (EZH2) is a histone methyltransferase and subunit of polycomb repressive complex 2 (PRC2)5. Within PRC2, EZH2 is responsible for the methylation of histone H3 at lysine 27 (H3K27) and is critical in the balance of differentiation and proliferation6 (Supplementary Fig. 1). EZH2 activity is increased where the SWItch/Sucrose Non-Fermentable (SWI/SNF) complex is lost7. The SWI/SNF complex is a chromatin remodeling complex present in all normal cells7. The SMARCB1(INI1) subunit acts as a tumor suppressor gene, and germline loss-of-function alterations pre-dispose patients to rhabdoid tumors8. INI1 opposes EZH2, so its loss and associated dysregulation of EZH2 has an oncogenic effect5,7,9. The same observation is true for other subunits of the SWI/SNF complex, including ARID1A and SMARCA45,9.

Dysregulated EZH2 is associated with poor prognosis and tumor progression, and has been identified in several solid tumor types such as breast, prostate, esophagus, stomach, thyroid, and endometrial cancers10,11. EZH2 gain-of-function mutations contribute to malignant transformation of germinal B cells in B-cell lymphoma12,13. EZH2 inactivation in vitro and in animal models10,14–18 suggests that EZH2 inhibition is a rational approach for SWI/SNF-dysregulated tumors.

There are no current therapeutic options specifically targeting the abnormal pathways for solid tumors harboring epigenetic driver alterations. Recommended treatments for metastatic disease are limited to cytotoxic chemotherapy or immunotherapies19,20. A diverse set SWI/SNF-altered diseases typically present in children, adolescents, and young adults and include atypical teratoid rhabdoid tumor (ATRT), MRT, SCCOHT, thoracic SMARCA4/BRG1-deficient undifferentiated tumors, RMC, poorly differentiated chordoma, epithelioid sarcoma, and synovial sarcoma21–26. In the advanced stages, limited systemic options are available and overall survival (OS) is uniformly poor23–25. Therefore, there is a clear unmet need for more effective and tolerable treatment options.

Tazemetostat (TAZ) is a first-in-class, selective oral inhibitor of EZH2 granted accelerated approved by the US Food and Drug Administration for the treatment of adult advanced epithelioid sarcoma (based on Cohort 5 of this basket study; previously published27) and relapsed or refractory follicular lymphoma28. A phase 1 multicenter study (NCT02601937) of pediatric patients with relapsed or refractory INI1-negative tumors has been published previously and suggest promising activity for TAZ29.

This basket study (NCT02601950) assessed the efficacy and safety of TAZ in solid tumors lacking INI1 or BRG1 expression or with EZH2 gain-of-function mutations, or in relapsed or refractory synovial sarcoma (Supplementary Fig. 2).

In this analysis we report the efficacy and safety of 800 mg BID TAZ in patients with SMARCB1/INI1- or SMARCA4/BRG1-deficient rhabdoid tumors (Cohort 1), relapsed or refractory SS18-SSX-fused synovial sarcoma (Cohort 2), INI1-negative or mutant EZH2 solid tumors (Cohort 3), RMC (Cohort 4), or poorly differentiated chordoma (Cohort 7). Interim data for Cohort 6 (epithelioid sarcoma) have been reported previously30, and Cohort 8 (epithelioid sarcoma, 1600 mg QD TAZ) will be reported separately. The data presented in this publication were generated while the product was under development and should be interpreted in that context. On 9 March 2026, Ipsen announced the voluntarily withdrawal of tazemetostat in all indications from all Ipsen markets including both for follicular lymphoma and epithelioid sarcoma. Ipsen's decision to withdraw is based on emerging data from the ongoing Phase Ib/III SYMPHONY-1 trial (evaluating tazemetostat in combination with lenalidomide plus rituximab vs rituximab in follicular lymphoma). The Independent Data Monitoring Committee advised that, based on adverse events of secondary hematologic malignancies, the risks may outweigh potential benefits for patients within this treatment regimen. The phase Ib/III SYMPHONY-1 trial will remain open, with discontinuation of tazemetostat treatment and with no further enrollment, to continue the long-term safety follow-up. All the other ongoing clinical trials for tazemetostat in all Ipsen markets were discontinued.

sec.title: Patients
sec.p: Between December 22, 2015, and September 10, 2021, the study enrolled 129 patients across 28 sites in 8 countries. These included 32 patients with INI1-deficient or BRG1-negative classic MRTs or SCCOHT in Cohort 1, 33 patients with SS18-SSX-fused synovial sarcoma in Cohort 2, 32 patients with INI1-negative or mutant EZH2 tumors in Cohort 3, 14 patients with RMC in Cohort 4, and 18 patients with poorly differentiated chordoma in Cohort 7.

Baseline demographics and disease characteristics are summarized for each cohort in Table 1. Across Cohorts 1–4 and 7, the median number of prior regimens in the advanced/metastatic setting was 1.0 (range, 0–11); 95% and 5% of patients, respectively, had Eastern Cooperative Oncology Group (ECOG) performance status of 0–1 and 2. The efficacy and safety populations comprised all patients who received at least 1 dose of TAZ.

sec.title: Treatment exposure
sec.p: All patients in Cohorts 1–4 discontinued TAZ prior to the data cutoff date of December 15, 2022, most commonly because of radiologic disease progression (Cohort 1: MRT or SCCOHT, 66% [21/32]; Cohort 2: synovial sarcoma, 79% [26/33]; Cohort 3: INI1-negative or mutant EZH2, 69% [22/32]; Cohort 4: RMC, 79% [11/14]; and Cohort 7: poorly differentiated chordoma, 39% [7/18]; Supplementary Fig. 3); 1 patient in Cohort 7 had ongoing TAZ treatment. Patients in Cohorts 1–4 and 7 received TAZ for a median (range) duration of 8.1 (1–84), 8.1 (2–51), 16.5 (1–144), 8.4 (3–44), and 18.1 (1–179) weeks, respectively. A small number of patients experienced a treatment-emergent adverse event (TEAE) resulting in withdrawal of study drug: 13% [4/32] in Cohort 1 and 6% in Cohort 7 [1/18].

sec.title: Efficacy
sec.p: Median duration of follow-up for the 32 patients with INI1-deficient or BRG1-negative classic MRTs or SCCOHT in Cohort 1 was 22 (range: 0.71–136.9) weeks. Overall treatment response and duration for each cohort is shown in Figs. 1 and 2. Objective response rate (ORR) was 9% (n = 3; 95% CI, 2–25), with 1 complete response (CR) and 2 partial responses (PRs; Table 2, [primary endpoint]). The patient who achieved a CR had BRG1-negative SCCOHT and a duration of response of 32.1 weeks. Of the 2 partial responders, 1 had SMARCA4-deleted NSCLC, and the other had BRG1-negative SCCOHT, with a duration of response of 29.0 and 24.1 weeks, respectively. 3 patients achieved disease control at 32 weeks; all of these were also patients who demonstrated a response to treatment. Durable responses were seen in 2/12 (17%) patients with SCCOHT.

sec.p: In 33 patients with synovial sarcoma (Cohort 2), median duration of follow-up was 42.9 (range: 9.9–149.3) weeks. 5 (15%) of 33 patients remained progression-free at 16 weeks (primary endpoint). No patients achieved CR or PR. However, 1 (3%) patient achieved disease control at 32 weeks (secondary endpoint).

In 32 patients with INI1-negative or mutant EZH2 tumors (Cohort 3), median duration of follow-up was 36.1 (range: 1.4–156.9) weeks. Results were not collected for the remaining 3 patients. ORR was 9% (n = 3; 95% CI, 2–25); all 3 patients had loss of INI1 expression and achieved a PR (primary endpoint). These responses were observed in patients with spindle cell tumor of the kidney, spindle cell sarcoma of the adrenal gland, and sinonasal carcinoma. Median duration of response in these 3 responders was 80.1 weeks (range: 24.1–87.6+, where ‘+’ denotes censored data as per the methods). Durations of response were 80.1 and 24.1 weeks for 2 patients, with 1 patient having an ongoing response at the time of data cutoff (and transferred into a long-term extension study). 6 patients achieved disease control at 32 weeks, of which 3 also achieved a partial response (secondary endpoints).

In 14 patients with RMC (Cohort 4), median duration of follow-up was 24.6 (range: 3.7–120.7) weeks. No patients achieved CR or PR. However, 1 patient achieved disease control at 32 weeks (secondary endpoint).

In 18 patients with poorly differentiated chordoma (Cohort 7), median duration of follow-up was 61.3 (range: 3.1–177.0) weeks. 1 (6%) patient with poorly differentiated chordoma had a PR (primary endpoint), with a duration of response lasting 151.6 weeks. 5 (28%) patients had RECIST responses and achieved disease control at week 32, including 1 patient with a PR (secondary endpoint).

Change from baseline in the sum of tumor diameters following treatment with TAZ in each cohort is shown in Fig. 1. In MRTs/SCCOHTs, median PFS was 7.9 (range: 0.1+–64.1) weeks (Fig. 3), and median OS was 22.1 (range: 0.7–136.9+) weeks (Table 2). In synovial sarcomas, median PFS was 8.0 (range: 2.0–54.9) weeks, with a 16-week PFS rate of 15.2 (95% CI: 5.1–31.9), and the median OS was 43.4 (range: 9.9–149.3) weeks. In Cohort 3, INI1-negative/EZH2-altered tumors, median PFS was 15.7 (range: 1.4–144.0) weeks, and median OS was 37.9 (range: 1.4–156.9+) weeks. In RMCs, median PFS was 7.3 (range: 0.1+–41.1) weeks, and median OS was 24.6 (range: 3.7–120.7+) weeks. In poorly differentiated chordomas, median PFS was 24.0 (range: 0.1+–175.3) weeks and median OS was 77.7 (range: 3.1–183.3+) weeks (secondary endpoints).

sec.title: Molecular/genomic analysis
sec.p: In Cohort 1 of patients with MRTs or SCCOHT, 8/32 (25%) patients had INI1 loss by local testing. In total, 23 patients showed BRG1 protein loss or BRG1 gene mutations by local testing. In the histology-agnostic Cohort 3, 29/32 (91%) patients were confirmed to have INI1 loss. In Cohort 4 of patients with RMC, 14/14 (100%) patients had INI1 loss by immunohistochemistry (IHC) locally. Similarly, in Cohort 7 INI1 loss was noted by local testing in all participants. Further genomic sequencing or attempts to assess changes in H3K27me3 marks deposited by EZH2 were not assessed in these tumor samples.
Results of the pharmacodynamic effects of TAZ in tumor tissue are described in Supplementary Note 1.

sec.title: Safety
sec.p: No deaths due to treatment-related adverse events occurred. TEAEs were reported in 123 (95%) patients (Table 3). Most common (≥20%) TEAEs in Cohorts 1–4 and 7 were nausea (31% [40/129]), fatigue (27% [35/129]), vomiting (26% [33/129]), dyspnea (25% [32/129]), cancer pain (24% [31/129]), and constipation (20% [26/129]). In total, 64/129 (50%) patients experienced a Grade 3/4 TEAE. Treatment-related adverse events (TRAEs) of Grade ≥3 were identified in 13/129 patients (10%). Anemia (3% [4/129]), decrease in lymphocyte count (2% [2/129]), and nausea (2% [2/129]) were the only Grade ≥3 TRAE reported in at least 2 patients. In 5 patients (4%; 4 female, 1 male), 7 serious TRAEs occurred that were related to TAZ (constipation, hyperbilirubinemia, nausea, pneumonia, soft tissue infection, and vomiting). Overall, TEAEs leading to dose reduction, drug interruption, or drug discontinuation occurred in 2% (2/129), 22% (28/129), and 5% (6/129) of patients, respectively.

sec.title: Discussion
sec.p: EZH2 inhibition by TAZ has limited antitumor activity in selected cancer types with molecularly defined alterations affecting the SWI/SNF chromatin remodeling complex resulting in unopposed hyperactivity of EZH2. TAZ did not provide benefit to patients with synovial sarcoma or RMC. However, there were signals of potentially promising activity in patients with SCCOHT and in other INI1-deficient tumors, such as a minority of patients with MRTs and in poorly differentiated chordoma.

These findings are important, given the rare and aggressive nature of the cancers investigated in this study and because of the critical unmet need of effective therapeutic options31. For instance, there is no standard approach to treatment of ATRT, with case series often describing multiple therapeutic approaches, including focal radiation and various intensities and combinations of chemotherapy32. Results from a phase 1 study evaluating TAZ monotherapy in pediatric relapsed or refractory INI1-negative tumors, including ATRT, showed promising results with ORRs of 24% (5/21) in ATRT, 33% (2/6) in poorly differentiated chordoma, 22% (2/9) in epithelioid sarcoma, and 0% in non–central nervous system rhabdoid tumors (n = 21) and other tumors (n = 6)29. Poorly differentiated chordoma is a rare aggressive tumor with dismal prognosis affecting children and young adults, often requiring multimodality treatment with no approved active systemic therapies33–36. Interestingly, in poorly differentiated chordomas, the loss of INI1/SMARCB1 is a primary event that occurs alongside the sustained activation of brachyury, suggesting a unique oncogenic cooperation. This makes poorly differentiated chordoma a unique entity, different from conventional or dedifferentiated chordoma, where INI1 loss is an acquired and less onco-relevant event and supports the evidence of TAZ activity in this type of sarcoma.

The molecular pathogenesis of SS18-SSX-fused synovial sarcoma is molecularly different from INI1- or BRG1-mutated tumors and may explain the lack of benefit observed with TAZ in this population37. The translocation alters the SWI/SNF complex in a way that mimics the effects of INI1 deficiency, leading to SOX2 activation38. In preclinical human models of synovial sarcoma, EZH2 inhibition did not lead to a significant change in SOX2 expression18.

Given that overactivation of EZH2 results from SWI/SNF dysfunction and is associated with promotion of tumorigenesis10, EZH2 inhibition could represent a promising treatment strategy for some patients with SWI/SNF-dysregulated tumors. In this multicohort basket study, TAZ yielded objective responses in 9% of patients with MRTs or SCCOHT (Cohort 1) or 9% with INI1-negative non-rhabdoid tumors (Cohort 3). Median duration of response in patients with MRTs or SCCOHT (Cohort 1) and in other non-rhabdoid tumors lacking INI1 mutations (Cohort 3) is notable (29.0 and 80.1 weeks, respectively). In the rhabdoid cohort, 2 patients were on treatment for over a year which is a remarkable outcome given the dismal prognosis associated with this disease. In Cohort 3 of INI1-/EZH2-altered tumors, 5 patients were on treatment for over a year and 3 patients were on treatment for over 2 years. In poorly differentiated chordoma (Cohort 7), 5 patients were on treatment for over a year and 2 patients were on treatment for over 2 years; 5 patients had radiologic evidence of tumor shrinkage (of <20%), and a RECIST PR was achieved in only 1 patient. Given the poor prognosis of the involved tumor types, these findings are remarkable for the durable stability offered by study treatment.

TAZ was well tolerated, with 10% of patients experiencing a Grade ≥3 TRAE, and few dose reductions (2%) or drug discontinuations (4%) with no deaths due to TRAEs. The safety profile of TAZ in the present analysis was consistent with that previously reported for patients with epithelioid sarcoma or follicular lymphoma39.

The clinical activity of TAZ in patients with INI1-negative epithelioid sarcoma was previously demonstrated in a single-cohort analysis of this multi-basket study27. Our study builds upon these findings by demonstrating that TAZ may provide some clinical benefit for patients with INI1-negative and BRG1-deficient solid tumors. This is especially important considering the lack of other effective therapies available for patients with INI1/BRG1-deficient tumors. By exclusively inhibiting EZH2, TAZ could potentially provide clinical benefit to patients with tumors harboring mutations in SWI/SNF subunits other than INI1 or BRG1. The decrease in EZH2 activity and potential dysregulation in differentiation and proliferation can be compensated for by EZH1, which co-mediates H3K27 methylation40. This raises the question as to whether dual EZH1/2 inhibitors may alternate signaling via EZH1. Kazansky et al. analyzed samples from responders and non-responders at a single institution revealing that resistance in a subset of INI1-deleted tumors may be mediated by mutations converging on the Rb/E2F signaling pathway41. This mechanism of resistance permits cells to escape TAZ-induced G1 arrest; to overcome this, the authors show combining TAZ with an inhibitor of aurora kinase B, which is downstream from Rb/E2F, or using a synthetic lethality strategy by leveraging ATR inhibition along with EZH2.

There are challenges with conducting a basket study of an EZH2 inhibitor epigenetic therapy, targeting components of the SWI/SNF pathway, namely SMARCB1 and BRG1. Limitations of the present analysis include the single-arm and nonrandomized design, as well as the small numbers of patients recruited to each cohort (n = 14–33). Notably, progression at study entry was only assessed by the investigators, and pre-study imaging was not evaluated as part of the study. There were few paired biopsies available, limiting the ability to correlate pharmacodynamic changes of protein expression with drug activity.

In conclusion, TAZ showed preliminary antitumor activity, with favorable tolerability, in rhabdoid tumors characterized by SWI/SNF dysfunction particularly SCCOHT and in poorly differentiated chordoma, whereas there was limited activity in patients with other tumors deficient in INI1 or BRG1, or with EZH2 gain-of-function mutations. These findings are encouraging, as standard treatments are lacking for rhabdoid tumors and other INI1- and BRG1-negative solid tumors. Further investigation into TAZ-based combination therapy in these tumor types may be warranted41. The data presented in this publication were generated while the product was under development and should be interpreted in that context. On 9 March 2026, Ipsen announced the voluntarily withdrawal of tazemetostat in all indications from all Ipsen markets including both for follicular lymphoma and epithelioid sarcoma. Ipsen's decision to withdraw is based on emerging data from the ongoing Phase Ib/III SYMPHONY-1 trial (evaluating tazemetostat in combination with lenalidomide plus rituximab vs rituximab in follicular lymphoma). The Independent Data Monitoring Committee advised that, based on adverse events of secondary hematologic malignancies, the risks may outweigh potential benefits for patients within this treatment regimen. The phase Ib/III SYMPHONY-1 trial will remain open, with discontinuation of tazemetostat treatment and with no further enrollment, to continue the long-term safety follow-up. All the other ongoing clinical trials for tazemetostat in all Ipsen markets were discontinued.

sec.title: Ethics statement
sec.p: The study was conducted in compliance and accordance with the Declaration of Helsinki, the International Conference on Harmonisation Guidelines for Good Clinical Practice, and applicable national and local regulatory requirements. The Independent Ethics Committee or Institutional Review Board at each participating site approved the protocol (Supplementary Note 3). All patients provided written informed consent prior to participation; travel reimbursement was made available to participants, no other compensation was provided. Archival tumor tissue, radiographic scans, and pretreatment biopsies were de-identified for central review and correlative studies.

sec.title: Study design and participants
sec.p: This study (NCT02601950) was an open-label, single-arm, multicenter, phase II basket study evaluating the efficacy and safety of TAZ 800 mg twice daily (Cohorts 1–7) or 1600 mg once daily (Cohort 8; not reported). The protocol is available at https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT02601950 (registered in October 2015). Patients were enrolled at 28 sites across the United States, Canada, the United Kingdom, France, Italy, Germany, Belgium, Australia, and Taiwan between December 22, 2015, and September 10, 2021. Enrollment was based on tumor type (Supplementary Fig. 2): rhabdoid tumors lacking INI1 or BRG1 (Cohort 1; includes malignant rhabdoid tumors, rhabdoid tumors of the kidney, ATRTs, and selected tumors with rhabdoid features, including SCCOHT), relapsed or refractory advanced synovial sarcoma with SS18-SSX rearrangement (Cohort 2), solid tumors lacking INI1 expression or with EZH2 gain-of-function mutations (Cohort 3; includes epithelioid malignant peripheral nerve sheath tumors, extraskeletal myxoid chondrosarcoma, myoepithelial carcinoma, other INI1-negative tumors with sponsor approval, and solid tumors including but not limited to Ewing sarcoma and melanoma), RMC (Cohort 4), epithelioid sarcoma (Cohort 5; previously published27), epithelioid sarcoma undergoing mandatory tumor biopsy (Cohort 6, previously published29), poorly differentiated chordoma (Cohort 7), or epithelioid sarcoma (Cohort 8).

Eligible patients were aged at least 18 years, with an ECOG performance status of 0–2, life expectancy of more than 3 months, and measurable disease per Response Evaluation Criteria in Solid Tumors (RECIST) v1.1 for solid tumors42 or Response Assessment in Neuro-oncology (RANO) criteria for brain tumors43. Patients were required to have loss of INI1 or BRG1 protein expression by IHC or biallelic INI1 or SMARCA4 alterations when IHC was unavailable (Cohorts 1, 3, 4, and 7); molecular evidence of EZH2 gain-of-function mutation (Cohort 3); or cytogenetics or fluorescence in situ hybridization (FISH) and/or molecular confirmation of SS18 rearrangement t(X;18) (p11;q11) (Cohort 2). Patients were enrolled based on local pathology results and provided tumor tissue for central confirmation of INI1 and BRG1 IHC and/or SS18 cytogenetics/FISH results and/or DNA mutation analysis. Key exclusion criteria included inadequate hematologic, renal, or hepatic function; active central nervous system or leptomeningeal metastasis of a primary extracranial tumor; previous malignancy, other than the disease under investigation; or Grade ≥3 thrombocytopenia, neutropenia, or anemia per Common Terminology Criteria for Adverse Events (CTCAE) 4.03 criteria. Progression before study entry was determined by the treating physician. Additional eligibility criteria are described in the protocol.

sec.title: Procedures
sec.p: Patients in Cohorts 1–4 and 7 who met the eligibility criteria received TAZ 800 mg BID, administered orally in continuous 28-day cycles until unacceptable toxicity, disease progression, or withdrawal of consent. Dose interruptions and reductions were permitted in the event of TEAEs, although no dose modifications were generally required for Grade 1 or 2 events (Supplementary Table S1). The protocol allowed up to 2 dose modifications, and treatment interruptions lasting more than 14 days and dose re-escalation were not permitted. Additional details are described in the protocol.

sec.title: Endpoints
sec.p: The primary endpoints were investigator-assessed ORR, defined as the percentage of patients with CR or PR per RECIST v1.1 or RANO criteria in Cohorts 1, 3, 4, and 7, and PFS at week 16, defined as percentage of patients with CR, PR, or SD at week 16, in Cohort 2. Secondary endpoints included ORR in Cohort 2, and duration of response (defined as time from the first objective response to disease progression or death from any cause), PFS (at weeks 24, 32, and 56, and overall; defined as time from first study treatment dose to disease progression or death), OS (at weeks 24, 32, and 56, and overall; defined as time from date of first study dose to death) and disease control rate (number of participants who achieved confirmed response or who have SD lasting at least 32 weeks), pharmacodynamic effects of TAZ in tumor tissue (results are described in the Supplementary Note 1), and safety and tolerability in Cohorts 1–4 and 7.

sec.title: Assessments
sec.p: Disease response was assessed every 8 weeks (regardless of treatment delays) or sooner, if clinically indicated. Radiographic scans (computed tomography and/or magnetic resonance imaging) were acquired at baseline and every 8 weeks thereafter and were evaluated by investigators per RECIST v1.1 or RANO criteria. A post-treatment visit was conducted within 30 (±3) days of the last dose of TAZ or prior to the start of alternate anticancer therapy. Patients who completed 2 years of treatment with TAZ were permitted to enroll in an open-label rollover study (TRuST; NCT02875548) to provide continued availability of treatment to those deriving clinical benefit. Patients who permanently discontinued TAZ were followed for survival every 16 weeks from the first dose of TAZ until death, withdrawal of consent, or loss to follow-up, or until the patient had been followed for 2 years. Adverse events, which were recorded throughout the study, were coded per Medical Dictionary for Regulatory Activities version 18.1 and graded per Common Terminology Criteria for Adverse Events version 4.03.

sec.title: Statistical analysis
sec.p: A 2-stage Green-Dahlberg design was utilized with a stopping rule to allow for early termination of each cohort at the end of Stage 1 if there was strong evidence of a lack of efficacy. The hypothesis was tested within each cohort using a 1-sided test, with an alpha of 0.05 and a type II error rate of 0.2. The Stage 1 interim analysis was performed after the first 15 patients completed at least the 16-week (Cohort 2) or 24-week (Cohorts 1, 3, 4, and 7) assessment, attended the final study visit, or terminated early, whichever occurred first (Supplementary Fig. 2). For the Stage 1 analysis of Cohorts 1, 3, 4, and 7 an ORR of less than 5% was indicative of futility, and more than 20% was indicative of potential efficacy. Following confirmation of potential efficacy in Stage 1, an additional 15 patients per cohort were enrolled to Stage 2. For the Stage 2 analysis of Cohorts 1, 3, 4, and 7, sufficient clinical activity was declared if at least 5 patients had confirmed CR or PR. For the Stage 1 analysis of Cohort 2, the rate of CR + PR + SD at week 16 of 15% or less was indicative of futility, and 35% or higher was indicative of potential efficacy. Following confirmation of potential efficacy in Stage 1, an additional 15 patients were enrolled to Stage 2. For the Stage 2 analysis of Cohort 2, sufficient clinical activity was declared if at least 9 patients had CR, PR, or stable disease. Over recruitment was permitted in cases where patients simultaneously signed informed consent at different sites. The ORR was calculated for the intent-to-treat population (all patients who received ≥1 dose of TAZ) of each cohort and was summarized using descriptive statistics, and the 95% exact binomial CIs around the point estimate. Null and alternate hypotheses for Stage 2 may be found in Supplementary Table S2.

Duration of response, PFS, and OS were estimated for each cohort using the Kaplan–Meier method. The 95% CI for PFS at week 16 in Cohort 2 was calculated using the exact binomial method. For other cohorts, PFS and corresponding 95% CIs at 24, 32, and 56 weeks were calculated using the Kaplan–Meier method with Kalbfleisch and Prentice complementary log–log transformation. The 95% CIs for median duration of response, PFS, and OS were calculated using the method of Brookmeyer and Crowley. Patients who continued TAZ after disease progression were censored at the time of progression.

The safety population comprised all patients in the intent-to-treat population who had at least one post-treatment safety assessment. Adverse events were summarized using descriptive statistics. The redacted study protocol amendment and Statistical Analysis Plan are provided in the supplementary information (Supplementary Note 4 and Supplementary Note 5, respectively).

Qualified researchers will be required to sign a data-sharing agreement with Ipsen before any release of such data. Upon signing the agreement, the data would be made available for the purpose(s) and duration specified in the agreement.

sec.title: Data Availability Statement
sec.p: The complete protocol of the study is available as Supplementary Note 5. Source data are not provided with this paper due to privacy restrictions related to study participant consent in the context of publications. Qualified researchers with a valid research question may request anonymized patient-level data by contacting an Ipsen representative. Further information on Ipsen’s Data Sharing policy is available here (Clinical Data Transparency - Global). Requests can be submitted via an Ipsen contact, or by emailing DataSharing@ipsen.com. Qualified researchers will be required to sign a data-sharing agreement with Ipsen before any release of such data. Upon signing the agreement, the data would be made available for the purpose(s) and duration specified in the agreement.
